visits.text: The scent of resin follows you along Lajų takas, the treetop walkway in the Anykščiai pine forest, 6 km from town. This 300 m walkway, opened in 2015, rises as high as 21 m above the ground. It ends at a 34 m tower. From the top, you can see the Šventoji River and the towers of the church in Anykščiai. Buy your €5 ticket at the information center at the base of the walkway, and save the tower for last.

According to a legend retold by the poet Antanas Baranauskas, the devil was carrying Puntukas, an enormous boulder, to crush the church in Anykščiai. A rooster crowed, and the devil dropped it along the way. Nearly 7 m long, it is Lithuania’s second-largest boulder. Glaciers brought it from the north. In 1943, during the German occupation, a sculptor secretly carved portraits of Darius and Girėnas into it. These Lithuanian aviators died in 1933 while attempting to fly nonstop from New York to Kaunas. The boulder is very close to the treetop walkway.

79 m: that is the height of each of the two towers of St. Matthew’s Church in Anykščiai, described as Lithuania’s tallest church. It was rebuilt in red brick from 1899 to 1909 in the Gothic Revival style, which imitates the Gothic architecture of the Middle Ages. Its original spires reached 84 m. They were destroyed during World War I. Come here after the treetop walkway: you’ll have seen the towers from a distance, and they look even taller up close.

The smallest museum in Anykščiai is worth a detour: Antanas Baranauskas’s klėtelė, a small wooden granary built in 1826 on the poet’s family farm. The writer Antanas Vienuolis-Žukauskas opened a museum here in 1927, described as Lithuania’s first memorial museum. Inside are the family’s furniture, belongings, and books. Baranauskas wrote The Forest of Anykščiai, a poem published in 1861 that became a Lithuanian classic. Allow 30 minutes: it’s a brief stop between two outdoor sites.

The Horse Museum in Niūronys, 6.5 km north of Anykščiai, shows the role of horses in Lithuanian rural life. Opened in 1978, it houses around 4,000 objects in 11 buildings. Horses live in the stables. A horseback ride around the enclosure costs €3. The museum is open daily, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from May through September and until 5 p.m. during the rest of the year. Adult admission costs €7.

activities.text: You’ll board Anykščiai’s little narrow-gauge train, nicknamed Siaurukas: its rails are only 75 cm apart. The line opened between 1895 and 1899. Anykščiai’s station and its water tower are protected as historic monuments. Inside the station, a museum displays a steam locomotive, a waiting room from the interwar period, and a handcar, a small rail cart propelled by pumping a lever. In season, trains also run to Lake Rubikiai. Check the current year’s schedule on siaurukas.eu before visiting.

days_plan.itin_title: Aukštaitija in 4 Days: Lakes, Stars, and Treetops

visits.text: Thousands of silver objects cover the walls of the chapel inside the Gate of Dawn (Aušros vartai), a former city gate. These are votive offerings, given in thanks for answered prayers: around 8,000 in all. They surround a painting of the Virgin Mary dating from around 1630, shown without the Christ Child and adorned with gilded silver. Built between 1503 and 1514, this is the only gate in the city walls to have survived their demolition from 1799 to 1805. The chapel opens daily at 7 a.m. The painting is also visible from the street: the chapel was designed so that people could pray outside.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

places.name: Druskininkai

visits.text: Brick red from its doorway to its bell tower, the Church of Our Lady of the Scapular stands at the beginning of Vilniaus Promenade in Druskininkai. Its name comes from the scapular, a small devotional garment worn over the shoulders. Warsaw architect Stefan Szyller designed it in the Gothic Revival style, which imitates medieval churches. Construction began in 1912 but was halted by World War I. The church was not completed until 1931. Outside the main tourist season, it often opens only for Mass: come during a service to see its brick arches.

Unassuming and built entirely of wood, the Orthodox church on Laisvės Square is nevertheless one of the oldest surviving wooden buildings in Druskininkai. It dates to 1865, when the town was part of the Russian Empire. Its silhouette also recalls the churches of Russia. It is dedicated to the “Joy of All Who Sorrow” icon, an image of the Virgin Mary venerated by Orthodox Christians. Stop by on a stroll: even with the door closed, the exterior is worth a detour.

Druska means “salt” in Lithuanian, and Druskininkai owes its name to it. As early as the 14th century, water from the saline springs was heated here to extract salt. Its salt content was too low for table salt production, so the water eventually came to be used for treatments. The Town Museum, housed in the former Villa Linksma on the shore of Lake Druskonis, tells the story of the spa town’s beginnings; it was recognized as a place for treatments on June 20, 1794. In a nod to the town’s name, the museum displays a record collection of salt shakers. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The brand-new Jacques Lipchitz Museum is our favorite in Druskininkai. Opened on April 17, 2026, at 17 Šv. Jokūbo Street, it traces the life of a local boy who became a sculptor in Paris and later New York. Born here in 1891, Lipchitz left for Paris in 1909. There he became a pioneer of Cubist sculpture, an art form that breaks bodies down into geometric volumes. The museum also tells the story of Druskininkai’s Jewish community. It is open Wednesday through Sunday, with last admission at 5:30 p.m.

Spa Park (Gydyklų parkas) is the oldest garden in Druskininkai. You can taste the mineral water at its drinking pavilion, the Springs Pavilion. Its stained-glass windows, by Kazys Morkūnas, illustrate a Lithuanian folktale: Eglė, a young woman who marries a serpent, eventually turns into a spruce tree. In the same park, water from the Beauty Spring rises from a depth of more than 300 m. It is the town’s saltiest spring, and its water is not for drinking. Sit in the drinking pavilion beside its small fountain to see the colored light from the stained glass.

activities.text: Follow the reproductions of paintings by Mikalojus Konstantinas Čiurlionis (1875–1911), a painter and composer, through the town center. He grew up in Druskininkai, where his father became the town organist in 1878. Many of his paintings are named after musical forms, such as sonatas or preludes: he also composed nearly 400 pieces. The route passes his monument, sculpted by Vladas Vildžiūnas in 1975. The reproductions line the “most visited places” route suggested by the Dzūkija tourism website.

Pine treetops pass beneath your feet, followed by the Nemunas: the Lynų kelias cable car crosses the river at a height of 45 m. The town describes it as Lithuania’s only cable car. Opened in 2015, it connects the water park to Snow Arena on the opposite bank in nearly 8 minutes. Snow Arena houses a 460 m indoor ski slope that has been open year-round since 2011. Take a round trip, even if you do not ski, for views over the Nemunas Valley.

If you walk along Vilniaus Promenade after dark, stop at the musical fountain at number 7. During the warmer months, its water jets dance every hour from 10 a.m. to 11 p.m. to a randomly selected tune. The show is free. For a fee, you can even choose the song by sending a text message. The fountain reopened in 2012, along with the renovated Spa Park.

Lake Druskonis lies right beside the Town Museum and the red church. Walk around it to see the spa town’s wooden villas, many of which have been restored. The oldest draw inspiration from Swiss chalets. Later villas follow the Zakopane style, named after a mountain resort in southern Poland. Some have been converted into rental apartments. Allow 45 minutes for the walk.

Set aside a late afternoon for Druskininkai Water Park (Vandens parkas), at 13 Vilniaus Promenade. Opened on December 26, 2006, it is Lithuania’s first water park. It has a family area and a separate adults-only area. In a town that has lived off spa treatments for more than two centuries, it is the easiest way to enjoy the water without booking a treatment. The cable car leaves from right next door: combine the two.

map_keywords: Druskininkų Švč. Mergelės Marijos Škaplierinės bažnyčia

visits.text: Puzzling—and that is its appeal—the Orvidas farm museum (Orvidų sodyba), 2 km from Salantai, brings together religious statues, boulders, carved tree trunks, and old tools in a large garden. Stonemason Vilius Orvidas began creating it in 1973, after serving in the Soviet army. He rescued stones and trees threatened with destruction by large-scale field drainage projects. Soviet authorities tried unsuccessfully to stop his project. A Soviet IS-2 tank has greeted visitors at the entrance since 1991. Admission is €8; the site is closed from December through February.

days_plan.itin_title: Samogitia in 3 Days: Lake Plateliai and Soviet Missiles

visits.text: If the sky is clear, save Gediminas Tower (Gedimino pilies bokštas) for the end of the day. It is the best-preserved part of the Upper Castle, a fortress dating from the 14th and 15th centuries. It crowns a 48 m hill, with views across the entire Old Town. The Lithuanian flag first flew here on January 1, 1919. The tower is open daily (€8). The inclined elevator at the foot of the hill broke down in 2025: if it is not running, take the path on the Vilnia side.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

visits.text: Things are buzzing at the Museum of Ancient Beekeeping in Stripeikiai, founded in 1984 by beekeeper Bronislovas Kazlas. Six buildings trace the history of the beehive, from hollowed-out tree trunks to modern frame hives. Outside, wooden sculptures honor Babilas and Austėja, the Lithuanian god and goddess of bees. Open May through September, Tuesday through Sunday; admission €6.

Stop at the Ginučiai watermill. This 19th-century mill produced flour until 1968. Its turbines also generated electricity for the village. It is the only one of the park’s six mills to retain its original equipment. Group tours of the interior are available by reservation; otherwise, climb the nearby hillfort, fortified between the 9th and 12th centuries.

If you climb just one hill in the park, choose Ladakalnis: an elevation of 176 m and views of six lakes. Its name is thought to come from Lada, a goddess worshipped before the arrival of Christianity. The climb is steep, starting from a parking lot in Ginučiai or Antalksnė. Visitors leave small stones: place them near the altar rather than at the foot of the oak tree, as the park requests.

days_plan.itin_title: Aukštaitija in 4 Days: Lakes, Stars, and Treetops

visits.text: “Stalin’s World” is the nickname of Grūtas Park (Grūto parkas), about 10 kilometers from Druskininkai. After regaining independence in 1990, Lithuania removed Soviet statues from its public squares. Businessman Viliumas Malinauskas obtained them from the state to display them rather than destroy them. He opened this open-air museum in 2001. Along two loops through the forest, 86 statues, including several of Lenin and Stalin, stand alongside watchtowers and barbed wire. The setting recalls the Gulag, the USSR’s forced labor camps. Allow 2 hours.

The small wooden museums in Grūtas Park are just as worthwhile as the statues. Propaganda posters, medals, and memorabilia from the Communist era sit alongside a recreated library with wax librarians. The gallery displays Socialist Realism, the official art of the USSR, which depicted happy workers and heroic leaders. In 2001, the park earned its creator the Ig Nobel Peace Prize, a parody of the Nobel Prizes that honors things that “first make people laugh, and then make them think.” Few signs are translated, so get the audio guide.

activities.text: Have lunch at the Grūtas Park café, which serves dishes and drinks described as “Soviet.” As in the rest of the park, the decor consists of objects from the era. From time to time, the park hosts actors who reenact official celebrations held under the USSR. Ask at the ticket office whether any entertainment is scheduled for the day of your visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Dzūkija in 3 Days: Druskininkai, Grūtas Park, and Zervynos

visits.text: Discover Kaunas, Lithuania's second-largest city set dramatically at the confluence of the nation's two mightiest rivers, the Nemunas and Neris. This historic city dating back to the 14th century served as Lithuania's temporary capital during the interwar period when Vilnius was under Polish control. Recently designated as a European Capital of Culture, Kaunas has undergone a remarkable renaissance that continues to transform its cultural landscape.

Explore Kaunas Old Town, a compact historic quarter where medieval streets open onto charming squares lined with Gothic and Renaissance architecture. Town Hall Square, dominated by the elegant white Town Hall nicknamed the “Swan”, has served as the city's heart for centuries. Surrounding streets reveal hidden churches, merchants' houses, and courtyards that whisper stories of the city's prosperous trading past.

Visit Kaunas Castle, one of the earliest stone fortifications in Lithuania, built in the mid-14th century to defend against the Teutonic Knights. Though partially ruined, the surviving tower and walls powerfully evoke the medieval conflicts that shaped Lithuanian history. The castle's strategic position at the river confluence underscores its military importance in defending the realm.

activities.text: Stroll along Laisvės Alėja (Liberty Avenue), one of the longest pedestrian streets in Europe stretching 1.6 kilometers through the heart of modern Kaunas. This elegant tree-lined boulevard connects the Old Town with the New Town, passing historic buildings, shops, and vibrant cafés. The avenue pulses with local life, offering an authentic glimpse into contemporary Lithuanian urban culture.

days_plan.itin_title: Lithuania Road Trip: Vilnius, Hills and Baltic Dunes
The Baltics: From Vilnius to the Dunes and Riga in 14 Days

visits.text: Five mounds in a misty valley: few know that Kernavė, inscribed on UNESCO's list in 2004, concentrates 10,000 years of human occupation on 194 hectares. It's the former political capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, abandoned in the 14th century after Teutonic Knight raids and never rebuilt. This sudden disappearance preserved intact this unique archaeological landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltics: From Vilnius to the Dunes and Riga in 14 Days

visits.text: Locals in Klaipėda call her Taravos Anikė, “Annette of Tharau”: she is the barefoot girl atop the fountain in Teatro aikštė, Theater Square. She represents a love poem written in 1636 by Simon Dach, a poet born in Klaipėda. In March 1939, Germany annexed the city, and Hitler came to give a speech. Legend has it that he had the statue removed because its back was turned toward the theater balcony. The 1912 original disappeared during the war; the current replica was based on old photographs. The square also hosts concerts and festivals: check the schedule.

Thick brick walls and passages beneath the ramparts: the Klaipėdos pilies muziejus, or Castle Museum, occupies two fortified gateways dating from the 16th through the 18th centuries and a restored rampart. The Teutonic Knights, a German military order, founded this castle in the mid-13th century. Its last bricks were dismantled in the 19th century and reused in houses in the old town. Since 2021, an exhibition inside the restored rampart has displayed nearly 5,000 objects found during excavations. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes; adult admission costs €6.

Until 1923, Klaipėda was officially called Memel, and the Mažosios Lietuvos istorijos muziejus, or History Museum of Lithuania Minor, tells the story of that past. Lithuania Minor was a region of former East Prussia inhabited by Lithuanians known as Lietuvininkai. The museum occupies one of the city's oldest Baroque houses, dating to 1774. Its galleries range from the graves of Baltic tribes to the first books printed in Lithuanian, with extensive coverage of everyday life among the Lietuvininkai. Allow 1 hour; adult admission is €4.

More workshop than display case, the Kalvystės muziejus, or Blacksmithing Museum, occupies the premises of blacksmith Gustav Katzke (1868–1944), complete with his bellows and forge hearth. You will see forged weathervanes typical of this port and iron grave crosses from the late 19th century. Some of the railings came from the city's former cemetery, now the sculpture park. With help from the staff, you can forge a small decorative piece yourself. Adult admission is €3.

If the sun is shining, save time for the garden at the Laikrodžių muziejus, or Clock Museum, on Liepų Street. A horizontal sundial lets you tell the time using your own shadow. Another shows Klaipėda's solar time, determined by the sun's position: compare it with your phone, as it does not match official local time. Inside, more than 400 clocks span the Renaissance through Art Nouveau, alongside replicas of water, fire, and sand clocks. The museum is closed on Mondays and stays open until 8 p.m. on Thursdays.

Klaipėda's former central post office, a Gothic Revival building on Liepų Street, houses a 48-bell carillon in its tower. A carillon is an instrument made of tuned bells that a musician plays from a keyboard. The first was installed here in 1987, and the current set weighs more than 5 tonnes. Short concerts take place at noon on certain weekend days; you can listen from the street. Ask the tourist office for the current schedule.

A peaceful park on the site of a former cemetery: Skulptūrų parkas, or Martynas Mažvydas Sculpture Park, occupies the municipal cemetery used from 1820 to 1959. More than 40,000 people were buried here, and a few graves are still visible. Modern stone sculptures began to be installed in 1977; the park now has 116. Admission is free at all hours. Allow 45 minutes to stroll along the paths at an unhurried pace.

The Danė waterfront, Danės krantinė, is at its best in the evening, when Klaipėda’s river reflects the colors of the sunset. The Meridianas, a sailing ship built in 1948 at the Turku shipyard in Finland, served as a training ship for sailors until 1968. Moored at the quay since 1969, it now serves as a restaurant. A little farther along, the riveted iron swing bridge from 1855 is still turned by hand: two people are enough to open it for boats. Finish with the old warehouses on Žvejų Street, reminders of the port’s past.

activities.text: You will soon notice that the streets of Klaipėda's old town, on the left bank of the Danė, are as straight as if drawn with a ruler. This grid plan is rare in Lithuania, where old towns tend to have winding lanes. Several houses retain their half-timbered facades, with exposed wooden framing, as in Germany. Walk between the museums: the old town is easy to explore without a car.

visits.text: Kretinga Manor became the residence of the Tyszkiewicz counts in 1875, when Józef Tyszkiewicz moved in with his family. Since the early 1990s, it has housed the Kretinga Museum. Seven rooms tell the story of this noble family through portraits, furniture, and photographs. Other rooms display the region’s folk art, including carved wooden crosses. The museum is open Wednesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Banana plants and cacti under glass, about twelve kilometers from the Baltic Sea: Kretinga’s winter garden (Žiemos sodas) is a surprise in this climate. Count Tyszkiewicz had it built around 1875 to connect two manor buildings beneath a 16 m glass roof. At the time, it was described as Europe’s largest private winter garden. Today, it houses about 3,800 plants representing 580 species, and has had a café since 1993. The garden is also open on Tuesdays, when the museum rooms are closed.

activities.text: You’ll finish with a stroll through the park at Kretinga Manor, which covers more than half of the estate’s 43 hectares. Look for the astronomical calendar: a sundial tells the time using the shadow of a rod. The original gardens were destroyed during World War II, and the present park has since been restored. Allow 30 minutes to explore its paths and fountain before getting back on the road.

days_plan.itin_title: Samogitia in 3 Days: Lake Plateliai and Soviet Missiles

visits.text: The Church of the Holy Trinity in Liškiava has a surprising Greek cross plan, with four equal arms beneath a dome. The Dominicans, an order of preaching friars, generally built long naves instead. Completed along with its monastery in 1741, the church houses seven Baroque and Rococo altars, the latter style featuring delicate, curving decoration. Its 1899 organ was played by Konstantinas Čiurlionis, the father of painter M. K. Čiurlionis. In the crypt, Dominican monks rest in glass-covered coffins. Open for visits Wednesday through Sunday, noon to 6 p.m., €3 per adult.

If you enjoy a view, climb Liškiava Castle Hill above the Nemunas. Grand Duke Vytautas had a stone castle built here. In 1410, Poland and Lithuania defeated the Teutonic Knights, German warrior monks who had been attacking the country, at Grunwald. With the threat removed, the castle remained unfinished: only part of a tower survives. According to legend, a fairy wanted to dam the river with the Witch’s Stone, but dropped it when a rooster crowed. The church is less than a kilometer away, so walk here.

visits.text: Just 140 meters long, yet honoring some 200 writers: Writers’ Street (Literatų gatvė) pays tribute to them on one of its walls. Each small artwork displayed there celebrates an author connected to Vilnius or Lithuania. The street’s name is thought to come from the printing houses and bookstores once located here. Another explanation points to Adam Mickiewicz, the great Polish and Lithuanian Romantic poet, who lived here in 1823. The narrow street leads onto Pilies Street, the Old Town’s main thoroughfare: the detour takes just a few minutes.

places.name: Marcinkonys

visits.text: Marcinkonys, a former forestry camp mentioned as early as 1637, is home to the Dzūkija National Park headquarters. Its visitor center at 61 Miškininkų Street presents the forest’s history, flora, and fauna, with admission costing €2. The center also provides information about the Čepkeliai Trail, located outside the village, where you can explore Lithuania’s largest peat bog. A peat bog is a wetland whose soil consists of accumulated dead moss. To take a guided tour of this trail, book through the center. The center opens Tuesday through Saturday, closing at 4 p.m. on Saturdays.

The house and barn at the Marcinkonys Ethnographic Farm Museum date from 1905. The museum, which opened in 1994, brings together objects collected in the park’s villages. You can see the equipment used by beekeepers who climbed pine trees to harvest honey from bee colonies living in the trunks. In the village, the wooden church with two towers, dedicated to Saints Simon and Jude, is worth a stop. The museum has no posted hours, so ask at the visitor center whether it is open.

days_plan.itin_title: Dzūkija in 3 Days: Druskininkai, Grūtas Park, and Zervynos

map_keywords: Dzūkijos National Park Visitor Center Marcinkonys

visits.text: Start the day at the Dzūkija National Park visitor center at 3 Vilniaus Street in Merkinė. Established on April 23, 1991, the park protects a vast pine forest, its rivers, and its villages of wooden houses. The center provides information on sights and accommodations, and admission to its exhibition costs €2. It also sells the visitor ticket, a voluntary donation of €5 per month toward the park’s upkeep. Open Tuesday through Saturday from 9 a.m., with a break from noon to 12:45 p.m.

From the top of Merkinė Hillfort (Merkinės piliakalnis), you can see two rivers meet: the Merkys flows into the Nemunas here. In the 13th century, a wooden castle surrounded by palisades stood on this partly artificial mound. The Teutonic Knights attacked it several times. In 1387, King Jogaila signed the charter here that granted Vilnius its city rights, meaning the right to govern itself. Park on Route 133 before the bridge, then take the footbridge. Access is free.

Standing 26 m tall, Merkinė Observation Tower offers sweeping views of the Nemunas Valley. From the top, you can see the confluence with the Merkys, Pastraujas Island, the bridge, and the town’s rooftops around the Church of the Assumption. Farther away, the forest recalls the Great Forest of old, where Lithuanian rulers came to hunt with their guests. The hillfort is close by, so compare the two viewpoints.

A museum inside a church that was itself built on the site of a town hall: Merkinė Regional Museum (Merkinės krašto muziejus) occupies the former Orthodox church on the central square. This church replaced the 16th-century town hall in the early 1880s. The exhibition traces the town’s history from the Stone Age onward. You will learn that Władysław IV Vasa, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania, died here in 1648. The exhibition also covers the 1945 attack by Lithuanian partisans against the Soviet occupiers. Open Tuesday through Saturday, admission €2.

days_plan.itin_title: Dzūkija in 3 Days: Druskininkai, Grūtas Park, and Zervynos

visits.text: It is nicknamed the Venice of Lithuania, and the name is no exaggeration: in Minija, also known as Mingė, the Minija River serves as the main street. The farmhouses on both banks, often dating from the late 19th century, face the water. No bridge connects the two sides: residents cross by rowboat. The village, documented as early as 1540, has never had a cemetery, and the dead were buried in Ventė. Come by car, as no public transportation serves the village.

If the sky is clear, stop at the lagoon observation tower on the road to Minija. It overlooks the Curonian Lagoon (Kuršių marios), a large body of water separated from the Baltic Sea by a long strip of dunes. The reed beds along the shore attract waterbirds. In the past, Minija residents cut reeds in winter from the frozen marshes of Kniaupas Bay to thatch their roofs. Bring binoculars and allow 20 minutes.

activities.text: You will truly understand Minija from the water. Village boat operators offer trips by reservation, including a loop of about 2 hours through Kniaupas Bay, the Curonian Lagoon, and the Atmata, a branch of the Nemunas, to the old Uostadvaris Lighthouse. The route and duration are arranged with the boat operator according to your preferences and the weather. The village also has a small marina for sailboats and motorboats.

days_plan.itin_title: Klaipėda and the Nemunas Delta in 3 Days: Villages on the Water

visits.text: It looks like a flying saucer set down in the countryside, but this is a serious museum: the Lithuanian Museum of Ethnocosmology in Kulionys, about 10 km from Molėtai. Ethnocosmology studies how different peoples understand the sky through their beliefs and calendars. The building echoes the cosmic tree of ancient myths: the underground gallery represents the roots, and a telescope crowns the tower. The guided tour lasts up to 1 hour 30 minutes and takes you up to the observation deck, 32 m above the ground. Book ahead: tours run Tuesday through Saturday, in Lithuanian or in English on request.

The Church of Saints Peter and Paul in Molėtai towers over the town center with its two tall towers. A church was mentioned here as early as 1522. The current building dates to 1905: a priest, Kazimieras Bandzevičius, designed it and had it built. The exterior is neo-Baroque, meaning it draws on the curves and elaborate ornamentation of the Baroque style. Inside, the altars are neoclassical, with straighter lines. Stop by just before your walk around the lakes, which starts a few hundred meters away.

214 spiral steps lead to the top of the 36 m Mindūnai Observation Tower, a 15-minute drive east of Molėtai. It stands within Labanoras Regional Park, a large protected expanse of forests and lakes. At the top, you’re level with the pine treetops. You can also see Lake Baltieji Lakajai, which the tourist office lists among the largest glacier-carved lakes in the eastern part of the country. Access is free and open at all hours: aim for late afternoon, when the light is soft.

activities.text: You’ll walk around Lakes Pastovis and Pastovėlis in the heart of Molėtai on a 4 km trail, or 5.5 km for the longer loop. Pedestrian bridges cross the water. Sculptures line the path, including a pair of fishing boots with a fishing rod and a fish wearing a saddle. Waterbirds abound along the shores. Start on Jaunimo Street and bring a swimsuit in summer: several swimming spots lie along the route.

If the sky is clear, end the day at one of the Museum of Ethnocosmology’s two telescopes, with diameters of 80 cm and 40 cm. The session lasts 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes. It starts about 1 hour 30 minutes after sunset, around 11:30 p.m. in late June. In mid-August, night falls 1 hour earlier. In August and September, you may see shooting stars. The museum confirms or cancels the session by 2 p.m. that day depending on the weather. Bundle up: the tower is just as cold as the outdoors.

days_plan.itin_title: Aukštaitija in 4 Days: Lakes, Stars, and Treetops

visits.text: Explore the Curonian Spit, a UNESCO World Heritage Site—a narrow peninsula of sand dunes stretching for 98 kilometers between the Curonian Lagoon and the Baltic Sea. This remarkable land formation, varying from just 400 meters to 4 kilometers in width, supports only a handful of villages surrounded by endless forests and spectacular shifting dunes.

Climb Parnidis Dune near Nida, one of the most impressive sand formations on the Curonian Spit rising up to 52 meters above sea level. The panoramic views from the summit encompass the vast lagoon, the Baltic Sea, and the forested dunes stretching toward the Russian border. A striking sundial sculpture marks the highest point, creating an iconic landmark against the ever-shifting sands.

Discover the Grey Dunes (also called the Dead Dunes or Agilos Dune) in Naglių Nature Reserve, haunting sand formations that once buried entire villages beneath their advancing masses. Following intensive logging in the 17th and 18th centuries, these dunes began to migrate inland, engulfing settlements along the way. Today, ongoing stabilization efforts preserve this ever-changing landscape, where the power of nature remains dramatically visible. Allow for a round trip from Nida to the parking lot, then reach the dunes on foot along the maintained trail.

activities.text: Walk through the pristine pine forests that anchor the dunes and provide habitat for diverse wildlife on this fragile peninsula. The contrast between dense woodland and open sand creates a surreal environment that shifts with the seasons and the winds. These forests represent centuries of careful management to prevent the dunes from consuming the entire spit.

Explore the charming fishing village of Nida, the largest settlement on the Lithuanian portion of the Curonian Spit, with its traditional wooden houses and colorful weathervanes. This picturesque village has attracted artists and writers for over a century, including Thomas Mann who built a summer home here. The peaceful atmosphere and unique light quality continue to inspire visitors from around the world.

days_plan.itin_title: Lithuania Road Trip: Vilnius, Hills and Baltic Dunes
The Baltics: From Vilnius to the Dunes and Riga in 14 Days

places.name: Okupaciju Ir Laisves Kovu Muziejus

visits.text: From 1944 to 1991, the KGB, the Soviet political police, occupied the building that now houses the Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights (Okupacijų ir laisvės kovų muziejus). It is nicknamed the “KGB Museum.” In the basement, you walk through the prison and former execution chamber. More than 1,000 people were executed here between 1944 and the early 1960s. The upper floors recount the deportations of Lithuanians to Soviet camps and the struggle of the “Forest Brothers,” partisans who hid in the woods. Open Wednesday through Sunday (€6), closing at 5 p.m. on Sunday.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

map_keywords: Museum of Occupations and Freedom Fights Vilnius

visits.text: A 19th-century palace in a botanical park to showcase amber: Palanga's Amber Museum is as unusual as it is successful. Housed in the Tiškevičius Manor, it displays more than 4,500 pieces of Baltic gold, including insect inclusions tens of millions of years old. The adjacent park—designed by French landscape architect Édouard André—is worth the visit alone.

Iodized air and pine resin mingled: Palanga and its 470-meter pier extend into a surprisingly calm Baltic Sea. The town is Lithuania's main seaside resort, with 16,000 winter inhabitants and summer crowds. The pedestrian Jono Basanavičiaus Street concentrates amber shops, restaurants, and old wooden villas. Sunset on the pier is mandatory.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltics: From Vilnius to the Dunes and Riga in 14 Days

places.name: Paluse

visits.text: In 1750, the priest Juozapas Baziliauskas had St. Joseph’s Church in Palūšė built on his own land near Lake Lūšiai. It is made of wood and was assembled without nails. Its eight-sided bell tower, added around 1800, echoes the watchtowers of old wooden castles. The church appeared on the back of the 1-litas banknote; the litas was the country’s former currency, replaced by the euro in 2015. To see it from a distance, stop at the Kaukiškė viewpoint, 8 km away along the park road: on a clear day, you can make it out beyond the lakes.

The Aukštaitija National Park visitor center in Palūšė features the exhibition “People of the Lakes.” It shows how residents fished, traveled by raft, and made their livestock swim across the lakes to reach pastures. Children can try their hand at fishing. Established in 1974, the park is Lithuania’s oldest national park. It has 126 lakes. The center is open Tuesday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.: ask the staff for advice on walks.

activities.text: Walk or bike along Lake Lūšiai on the 2 km gravel path connecting Palūšė to the village of Meironys. Along the water, 14 wooden sculptures carved in 1977 by folk artists tell the park’s legends. Several depict devils: local elders say one still lives in nearby Lake Taramas. Continue onto the Meironys trail, whose 3.7 km yellow loop crosses two hills overlooking the lake. Wear sturdy shoes, as the path climbs and descends constantly.

On Lake Lūšiai in the morning, only the sound of a paddle breaks the silence. Rent a kayak or rowboat at Palūšė’s boating center, Palūšės valtinė, or a paddleboard from Tiki Tours in the same village. More athletic visitors can follow the Great Loop, a 28 km circuit through lakes and streams designed to take two or three days. For a half-day outing, stay on Lake Lūšiai. From May through October, the boat Kajsa also takes up to 12 passengers on trips from Palūšė.

days_plan.itin_title: Aukštaitija in 4 Days: Lakes, Stars, and Treetops

map_keywords: Aukštaitijos nacionalinio parko lankytojų centras Palūšė

visits.text: Big noses, bulging eyes, toothless mouths: more than 300 wooden masks grimace in the former stables of Plateliai Manor. They are worn during Užgavėnės, the Lithuanian carnival before Lent, the weeks of fasting leading up to Easter. At the start of the celebration, Morė, an effigy representing winter, is burned. If you visit in February or March, you can attend the celebration in town. The mask exhibition is closed on Mondays; admission costs €6.

The granary at Plateliai Manor houses the exhibition for Samogitia National Park, established in 1991. It traces the history of the manor, the old town, and Castle Island, then introduces the park’s natural environment. Until 1940, the estate belonged to the Choiseul-Gouffiers, a family of French counts. In the 19th century, Sophie de Choiseul-Gouffier lived here and wrote in French. The manor’s main wooden house burned down in 1943: only its foundations remain visible. On weekdays outside summer, the exhibition closes from noon to 1 p.m.

The town’s loveliest surprise may be the entirely wooden Church of Saints Peter and Paul in Plateliai. Built in 1744 from squared logs—tree trunks hewn at right angles—it replaced three earlier churches. Its wooden bell tower houses a bell dated 1648. Look at the Rococo pulpit, an example of the curving decorative style of the 18th century. Two members of the Choiseul-Gouffier family, former owners of the manor, are buried in the surrounding cemetery. Enter quietly if Mass is in progress.

According to Plateliai legends, witches gather at night beneath the Witches’ Ash (Raganos uosis) in the manor park. It is Lithuania’s largest ash tree: 7.2 m in circumference, 32 m tall, and more than 200 years old. Another legend explains its enormous trunk: the devil supposedly squeezed four ash trees together until they fused into one. The park is also the national park’s largest bat refuge, home to seven species. In summer, linger at dusk as they emerge to hunt.

activities.text: You’ll follow the shore of Lake Plateliai along the Šeirė Trail (Šeirės pažintinis takas), a 4.1 km loop starting 1.3 km from the park’s visitor center. It crosses the Gaudupis peat bog, a wetland where dead moss accumulates in thick layers. A viewing platform then overlooks the lake and its seven islands. This is Samogitia’s largest and deepest lake. In the 15th century, the dukes of Lithuania had a castle on Castle Island, connected to the shore by a wooden bridge. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the walk.

Small tower, big view: the Siberija observation tower is only 15 m tall, but it stands atop Cidabras Hill. From the top, you can see two lakes, Plateliai and Beržoras, as well as Siberija Marsh. The view also takes in the village of Beržoras and Liepija Forest. Visit late in the day, after the manor park and its ash tree.

A heel print marks a 4.5 m boulder: this is the Devil’s Foot Stone on the sacred hill of Mikytai, 11 km north of Plateliai. According to legend, the devil destroyed a church built there, then left this mark as he fled. This hill, called Alka, was a sacred site long before Christianity arrived. The 1 km Mikytai Trail also passes the “Well of Prayers,” a hollow where a spring once flowed. Park near the road connecting Barstyčiai and Salantai.

days_plan.itin_title: Samogitia in 3 Days: Lake Plateliai and Soviet Missiles

visits.text: Peaceful forest above, nuclear missiles below: welcome to the Plokštinė base. From 1963 to 1978, the Soviet army kept four R-12 missiles ready for launch here, each a 23 m rocket armed with a nuclear bomb. Each stood at the bottom of a concrete silo about 30 m deep. Each bomb was more than a hundred times as powerful as the one dropped on Hiroshima. The missiles could reach Western Europe. The Cold War Museum (Šaltojo karo ekspozicija) takes you down into the command post, then lets you look into a missile silo without descending to the bottom. Open daily (€12); if you visit without a guide, get the audio guide (€4).

activities.text: If you have another hour after the museum, take the Plokštinė Trail (Plokštinės pažintinis takas), a 3 km loop starting beside the entrance. It crosses the former military grounds, where more than 10,000 soldiers worked in secret beginning in 1960. The site was not chosen at random. The sandy soil was easy to dig, and a 2.5 km pipeline brought water from Lake Plateliai to cool the facilities. Wear closed-toe shoes: the trail is mostly packed dirt.

days_plan.itin_title: Samogitia in 3 Days: Lake Plateliai and Soviet Missiles

visits.text: Rokiškis Manor alone is worth the trip north. Built in 1801 for Count Ignotas Tyzenhauz, it was remodeled in 1905 in a mix of styles ranging from Baroque Revival to Art Nouveau. The regional museum inside tells the story of its owners and local history. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; admission €8.

A small building, an immense body of work: Lionginas Šepka’s wood carvings fill six rooms in an annex at Rokiškis Manor. This local sculptor carved around 3,000 pieces, including scenes with dozens of figures. The exhibition ends with his final work, left unfinished. Allow 45 minutes after visiting the manor.

St. Matthew’s Church in Rokiškis stands on the main square. A kilometer-long pedestrian path connects it to the manor. Count Rajnold Tyzenhauz and his sister had it built between 1866 and 1885, with a 56.5 m spire. Inside, look for the Austrian stained-glass windows and the gilded bronze altar from France. Free admission, daily from 9 a.m. to 6:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Aukštaitija in 4 Days: Lakes, Stars, and Treetops

visits.text: Town Hall Square (Rotušės aikštė) has hosted markets and celebrations since the 15th century. It lies at the heart of the Old Town, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, and Classical facades stand side by side along its medieval streets. The columned town hall was redesigned between 1785 and 1799 by Laurynas Gucevičius, the cathedral’s architect. A few steps away on Didžioji Street, look up at the dome of St. Casimir’s Church, the city’s oldest Baroque church: it is topped with a crown.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

visits.text: This is the best introduction to the delta: the visitor center for Nemuno deltos regioninis parkas, the Nemunas Delta Regional Park, in Rusnė. Established in 1992, the park protects the area where the Nemunas splits into several branches before flowing into the lagoon. An interactive map shows trails and sights, and a motion chair lets you experience the sensation of a bird in flight. The center opens only on weekdays: from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Thursday, and until 3:45 p.m. on Friday.

A church that once served as a gym: Rusnės evangelikų liuteronų bažnyčia, a brick Lutheran church consecrated in 1809, housed a gym and a boiler room during the Soviet era. Services resumed in 1991. The town of Rusnė stands on Lithuania’s largest island, surrounded by branches of the Nemunas. One spot on the island even lies below sea level, the lowest point in the country. In the evening, walk along the Pakalnė River to the small harbor.

The statue of Mahatma Gandhi and Hermann Kallenbach, unveiled in Rusnė in 2015, is an unexpected sight in this town founded by fishermen. Kallenbach, an architect born in 1871 in Žemaičių Naumiestis, in the Šilutė district, went to work in South Africa. There he met Gandhi in 1904 and became his close friend. In 1910, he gave him a farm near Johannesburg, named Tolstoy Farm, where the families of his fellow nonviolent activists lived. Ten minutes is enough for a stop as you walk through town.

In 1907, a steam engine began pumping water from the Uostadvaris meadows into the Atmata, a branch of the Nemunas. This pumping station, the first of its kind in Lithuania, drained a polder: a low-lying area enclosed by dikes from which water must be pumped out. Right next door stands Uostadvario švyturys, a red brick lighthouse from the 1870s that was decommissioned in 1986. The station is privately owned: admire it from outside, from the dike.

activities.text: You’ll walk along the polder dikes, the best vantage points for observing wildlife in these lowlands. Pakalnės pažintinis takas, the Pakalnė nature trail, winds between the Pakalnė and Rusnaitė rivers through floodplain meadows. This interpretive trail explains how people drained these lands and how that changed the natural environment. Roe deer, moose and, during migration, many birds frequent these plains. Bring boots in spring: the ground stays waterlogged.

days_plan.itin_title: Klaipėda and the Nemunas Delta in 3 Days: Villages on the Water

places.name: Siauliai

visits.text: Experience the Hill of Crosses, one of the most extraordinary and spiritually powerful sites in the world, where hundreds of thousands of crosses cover a small hill in the Lithuanian countryside. This remarkable place began in the early 19th century when people placed crosses to commemorate loved ones who died in uprisings against the Russian Tsar. Despite repeated Soviet attempts to destroy it—removing crosses, closing roads, even trying to flood the area—the faithful continued placing crosses under cover of darkness, transforming the hill into an enduring symbol of resistance and faith.

Witness the incredible density and variety of crosses in all shapes and sizes, from tiny crucifixes to elaborate wooden sculptures several meters tall. The site became an important pilgrimage destination after Pope John Paul II celebrated Mass here in 1993, further cementing its significance in Catholic tradition. Walking among the countless crosses, rosaries, and religious statues creates an overwhelming sensory and spiritual experience unlike any other in the world.

activities.text: Take time to absorb the profound atmosphere of this unique sacred site, where faith and history intertwine in the most tangible way imaginable. Many visitors choose to add their own cross to the collection, continuing a tradition that spans over two centuries. The Hill of Crosses stands as a testament to the indomitable spirit of the Lithuanian people and their unwavering commitment to religious freedom.

days_plan.itin_title: Lithuania Road Trip: Vilnius, Hills and Baltic Dunes
The Baltics: From Vilnius to the Dunes and Riga in 14 Days

map_keywords: Pope John Paul II Mass Šiauliai

visits.text: Šilutės Hugo Šojaus muziejus, the Hugo Scheu Museum (Šojus in Lithuanian), occupies the manor house built in 1818 that this landowner of German origin bought in 1889. Scheu donated land to the town for the hospital, high school and post office. He also opened the Klaipėda region’s first museum in two rooms of the manor house. Much of his collection disappeared in 1944, when the Red Army occupied the estate. Allow 1 hour; the museum opens Tuesday through Saturday, and also on Sundays from May through August.

One hundred four faces look out at you from the altar wall of Šilutės evangelikų liuteronų bažnyčia, the Lutheran church in Šilutė, consecrated in 1926. This 80 m² mural brings together saints, reformers, scholars and craftspeople. Among them is Hugo Scheu, holding a model of the church, for which he donated the land. Outside, the 50 m tower bears Lithuania’s largest church tower clock. The interior is mainly open during services: ask the tourist office to arrange a visit.

activities.text: You’ll then stroll along Lietuvininkų gatvė, Šilutė’s main street, laid out in the 19th century between the old market square and the Žibai neighborhood. Its large Art Nouveau buildings are half hidden behind lindens and horse chestnuts. Until 1910, Šilutė was just a group of four villages, including Heydekrug, which gave the town its German name. Allow half an hour on foot before taking the road back to Klaipėda.

days_plan.itin_title: Klaipėda and the Nemunas Delta in 3 Days: Villages on the Water

visits.text: St. Anne’s Church (Šv. Onos bažnyčia) has a red brick facade as intricate as lace. Built around 1495–1500, it is an example of Flamboyant Gothic, the final phase of Gothic architecture, with decoration that ripples like flames. Its builders used 33 types of bricks. According to legend, Napoleon wanted to carry it back to Paris “in the palm of his hand” in 1812. The reality is less flattering: his soldiers used it as a warehouse and stable. The Baroque interior is open on Sundays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., but only in the late afternoon on weekdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

places.name: Sv Petro Ir Povilo Baznycia Vilnius

visits.text: Angels, demons, skulls, and strange creatures: some 2,000 figures made of stucco, a plaster molded in relief, cover the Church of St. Peter and St. Paul (Šv. apaštalų Petro ir Povilo bažnyčia). Military commander Michał Kazimierz Pac commissioned its construction starting in 1668 and brought in Italian stucco craftsmen. Beneath the dome, the chandelier is shaped like a boat because St. Peter was a fisherman. In accordance with his wishes, Pac lies buried beneath the entrance threshold. His tombstone, mounted on the right-hand wall, reads in Latin, “Here lies a sinner.” Admission is free, daily until around 6:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

map_keywords: Šv. apaštalų Petro ir Povilo bažnyčia
Church of St. Peter and St. Paul Vilnius

visits.text: Plain on the outside, surprising within: the Cathedral of St. Anthony of Padua in Telšiai saves its decoration for the interior. Franciscan monks built it in brick between 1762 and 1794 on Insula Hill, the highest point in the old town. It became a cathedral in 1926, when the Diocese of Telšiai was established. Look up at the galleries running along the upper level: three altars stand there, above those below. Visit outside Mass times to explore freely.

More than 62,000 objects tell the story of Samogitia, the historic region of northwestern Lithuania, at the Alka Museum (Žemaičių muziejus “Alka”). A local society of history enthusiasts founded it in 1932. The displays range from Lithuania’s earliest archaeological finds to furniture and paintings from the region’s manor houses. Some of the books and valuable objects from Plateliai Manor, seized by the state in 1940, were transferred here. The museum is closed on Mondays: allow 1 hour 30 minutes for your visit and budget €8 for admission.

In the Jewish world, Telšiai was known as Telz. The Telz Yeshiva, an institution of advanced Jewish learning founded in 1875, became one of Eastern Europe’s major centers of Jewish education. It was the first in Lithuania to introduce an entrance exam and classes grouped by level. Closed at the beginning of World War II, it was reestablished in 1942 in Cleveland, in the United States, where it still teaches today. Since 2023, its building in Telšiai has housed a museum about the city’s Jewish community. Check its hours on the website of the Alka Museum, which oversees it.

The Samogitian Village Museum (Žemaitijos kaimo muziejus) recreates rural life of the past on the southwestern shore of Lake Mastis. Sixteen 19th-century rural buildings, furnished and stocked with tools, are spread over 8.5 hectares. You’ll see three complete farmsteads, a mill, and a forge. From May through October, it opens daily (€5); from November through April, only on weekdays. Wear comfortable shoes: the buildings are scattered throughout a large park.

activities.text: Benches, docks, and illuminated paths: the shore of Lake Mastis serves as a large public garden for Telšiai. A network of trails circles the lake, with a sculpture park, a marina, and a developed beach. Look for the six carved bear cubs on the bridges: one is hiding, another is climbing, and a third lies dreaming. The bear is an ancient symbol of Samogitia. Toward the end of the day, climb Zakso Hill beside the lake for views of the city and the water.

You’ll explore the old town by following the Telšiai Seven Hills Route. Like Rome, the city is built on seven hills, as the tourist office points out. On Mill Hill, St. Nicholas Orthodox Church (1937) is considered Lithuania’s only Cubist church, meaning it is built from simple geometric forms. According to legend, the knight Džiugas founded the city, and one hill bears his name. The full route covers 9 km on paved surfaces and takes about 4 hours: stick to the central hills if you’re short on time.

days_plan.itin_title: Samogitia in 3 Days: Lake Plateliai and Soviet Missiles

visits.text: Red brick on green water: Trakai Castle rises from its island in the middle of Lake Galvė like a Gothic apparition. Built by Duke Kęstutis in the late 14th century and completed by Vytautas the Great around 1409, it served as the royal residence and state treasury of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. After centuries of ruin, restoration in the 1950s-1960s returned its medieval bearing.

activities.text: Rent a kayak from the Karaite village dock to circle the castle from the water: the perspective from the lake is incomparable. Lake Galvė has 20 islands—the full loop by kayak takes 1.5 hours. Avoid July weekends when boats compete for space.

days_plan.itin_title: The Baltics: From Vilnius to the Dunes and Riga in 14 Days

visits.text: Climb through Kalnai Park (Park of Hills) to the Hill of Three Crosses (Trijų kryžių kalnas): from its platform, the Old Town spreads out at your feet. According to legend, seven Franciscan monks were killed here by pagans. A first concrete monument was erected here in 1916, then demolished by the Soviet authorities on May 30, 1950. The current three white crosses, 12 m tall, were unveiled on June 14, 1989. Debris from the 1916 monument still lies a few meters below. In the evening, the crosses are sometimes lit in colors for events.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

visits.text: Vilnius’s most whimsical neighborhood lies across the Vilnia: Užupis, meaning “beyond the river” in Lithuanian. Its residents proclaimed it a “republic” on April 1, 1997, April Fools’ Day. Its constitution is displayed in 23 languages on a wall on Paupio Street. One article states: “A dog has the right to be a dog.” Run-down until 1990, the neighborhood is now home to nearly a thousand artists. An angel has been blowing a trumpet in the central square since 2002. Every April 1, “independence” is celebrated at its feet.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

places.name: Valdovu Rumai

visits.text: Although it looks old, the Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania (Valdovų rūmai) was rebuilt between 2002 and 2018. The original, the residence of Lithuania’s rulers, had been almost entirely demolished in 1801. The first visitor route traces the site’s history through archaeological excavations. A second (€10) takes you through rooms reconstructed in the palace’s successive styles, beginning with Late Gothic. In 1634, this palace hosted the first opera performed in Lithuania. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours. Leave your bag and bottle at the coat check: drinks are prohibited in the rooms.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

map_keywords: Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania

visits.text: In September and October, hundreds of thousands of migrating birds may fly over Cape Ventė in a single day, as many follow the eastern shore of the Curonian Lagoon. The Ventės rago ornitologinė stotis, an ornithological station founded in 1929 at the initiative of zoologist Tadas Ivanauskas, catches some of them in very large net traps. A numbered band is fitted to each bird's leg: if it is caught elsewhere, its journey can be traced. Exhibition admission is €4; it is generally open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Mondays.

An ornate iron staircase, a small platform, and water as far as the eye can see: the Ventės rago švyturys, or Cape Ventė Lighthouse, is one of the few lighthouses in Lithuania you can climb. This 19th-century red-brick tower stands 11 m tall. From the top, you can see the lagoon, the Curonian Spit opposite, and Rusnė Island. Below, a 250 m breakwater breaks up the ice at the end of winter, protecting the tip of the cape from erosion. Climb up in the late afternoon, when the light skims across the water.

You will pass through Kintai, a fishing village beside the lagoon, on your way to the cape. The Vydūno kultūros centras, or Vydūnas Cultural Center, occupies the former school built in 1705 where Lithuanian writer and philosopher Vydūnas taught from 1888 to 1892. It houses a small museum devoted to him and a gallery dedicated to enamel art. In the same village, the Great Church of Kintai served as an agricultural warehouse during the Soviet era before becoming a concert hall in 1987. Ask the Šilutė tourist office about opening hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Klaipėda and the Nemunas Delta in 3 Days: Villages on the Water

visits.text: A paving stone in the square in front of Vilnius Cathedral (Vilniaus arkikatedra) bears the name “Stebuklas,” Lithuanian for “miracle.” It marks one end of the Baltic Way: on August 23, 1989, around two million people joined hands from Tallinn, Estonia, to Vilnius in protest against Soviet rule. The cathedral has resembled an ancient temple since its reconstruction by Laurynas Gucevičius from 1783 to 1801. The Soviets turned it into a warehouse; Mass resumed there in 1988. Step inside the marble-clad Baroque Chapel of St. Casimir.

activities.text: Descend beneath Vilnius Cathedral on a guided tour of the crypts: this is the only way to enter them. You will see one of Lithuania’s oldest murals, painted around 1400. Beneath the Chapel of St. Casimir, the royal mausoleum houses Grand Duke Alexander Jagiellon and two wives of King Sigismund Augustus. The heart of King Władysław IV Vasa is also kept here. An empty sarcophagus still awaits Grand Duke Vytautas, who died in 1430: the search for his remains continues. Book ahead: the tour lasts 1 hour and costs €12.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

visits.text: The Old Town’s loveliest surprise lies behind the gates of Vilnius University (Vilniaus universitetas). The Jesuits founded it in 1579 under a charter from Stephen Báthory, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania. Its buildings are arranged around 13 courtyards, open Monday through Saturday from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. From spring through fall, climb the bell tower of St. John’s Church, the tallest building in the Old Town, by taking 193 steps or the elevator (€5). While the church roof is being renovated, with work scheduled to continue through the end of 2027, enter from Universiteto Street.

days_plan.itin_title: Vilnius in 2 Days: Baroque Old Town and Užupis

places.name: Vilnius

visits.text: Explore Vilnius Historic Center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that has preserved its remarkable medieval layout despite centuries of conflict and destruction. This atmospheric Old Town showcases an impressive architectural tapestry blending Gothic, Baroque, Renaissance, and classical styles across its winding cobblestone streets. The concentration of historic buildings within such a compact area makes Vilnius one of the best-preserved medieval urban centers in Eastern Europe.

Marvel at the stunning St. Anne's Church, a Gothic masterpiece of red brick architecture that has stood for over 500 years. Next to it stands the Church of St. Francis of Assisi (Bernardine), forming an impressive group of church buildings. Legend holds that Napoleon was so enchanted by St. Anne's beauty that he wished to carry it to Paris in the palm of his hand.

Pass through the Gate of Dawn, the only surviving gate of the original city wall and home to a revered icon of the Virgin Mary that draws pilgrims from across the Catholic world. This 16th-century gate once formed part of the city's defensive fortifications and now stands as both a religious shrine and architectural landmark. The chapel above the gate houses the miraculous painting venerated for centuries.

Wander along Pilies Street, the main artery of Vilnius Old Town connecting the Cathedral to the Gate of Dawn through the historic heart of the city. This vibrant pedestrian thoroughfare is lined with baroque buildings housing cafés, galleries, and shops selling amber and Lithuanian crafts. Street musicians and outdoor art exhibitions bring this ancient route to life throughout the year.

Discover the Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania, an exceptional museum housed within the meticulously restored 15th-century royal residence at Cathedral Square. The underground ruins of the original palace provide a fascinating archaeological journey, while upper floors display authentic furniture, tapestries, and paintings from Lithuania's golden age. The museum's cutting-edge 3D virtual reality experience transports visitors through centuries of Vilnius history in breathtaking detail.

Ascend to Gediminas Castle Tower, one of Lithuania's most treasured national symbols and the remaining vestige of the former Upper Castle. Grand Duke Gediminas established the first wooden fortifications here in the 14th century, founding what would become the Lithuanian capital. According to a beloved legend, Gediminas dreamed of an iron wolf howling from this hill, and a priest interpreted the dream as a prophecy of a great city whose fame would spread throughout the world.

Admire the grand Vilnius Cathedral and its distinctive Bell Tower standing proudly in Cathedral Square at the heart of the city. This neoclassical cathedral, rebuilt multiple times over seven centuries, serves as the principal Roman Catholic church of Lithuania. The freestanding Bell Tower, once part of the city's fortifications, has become an iconic landmark visible across the Old Town.

Explore the historic Vilnius University complex, one of the oldest and most renowned universities in Eastern Europe, founded in 1579. The university's thirteen interconnected courtyards showcase architectural styles spanning four centuries, from Gothic to Baroque. The magnificent Church of St. Johns within the complex features a stunning Baroque interior and a tower offering panoramic city views.

Visit Trakai Island Castle, a beautifully restored 14th–15th-century fortress rising from a small island in the crystal-clear waters of Lake Galvė. This Gothic red-brick castle, surrounded by an archipelago of 21 islands, stands as one of Lithuania's most photographed monuments and a powerful symbol of the nation's medieval grandeur. In the days of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, when the kingdom stretched from the Baltic to the Black Sea, Trakai served as one of the main political centers. Allow for a round trip from Vilnius for this visit to Trakai.

activities.text: Join a walking or cycling tour with local guides to uncover hidden stories and fascinating history beyond the main tourist sites. Expert guides reveal the layers of Vilnius history, from medieval grand dukes to Soviet occupation and the singing revolution that led to independence. These tours provide invaluable context that transforms a simple sightseeing walk into a deeper understanding of Lithuanian culture and resilience.

Rent a rowboat or kayak to explore the magnificent lake scenery surrounding Trakai Castle from the water. The area encompasses more than 30 lakes connected by channels, creating a unique aquatic setting perfect for peaceful paddling. Gliding across Lake Galvė offers the most spectacular views of the castle rising from its island setting. Allow for a round trip from Vilnius for this activity in Trakai.

Soar above Trakai in a hot-air balloon for an unforgettable aerial perspective of the castle, lakes and surrounding forests. From above, the full beauty of this lake region unfolds as a mosaic of water, islands and forests stretching to the horizon. This magical experience offers photographs and memories that last a lifetime. Allow for a round trip from Vilnius for this activity in Trakai.

visits.text: Since 1643, a painting brought from Rome has drawn pilgrims to Žemaičių Kalvarija. This Madonna and Child, believed to be miraculous, is displayed in the Basilica of the Visitation, a brick church built between 1780 and 1822. In 2006, Pope Benedict XVI blessed the crowns placed on the painting. A pilgrimage celebration takes place in the basilica on the 2nd of every month: choose that day for the atmosphere, or another for peace and quiet.

activities.text: You’ll follow the Way of the Cross in Žemaičių Kalvarija, laid out by Dominican monks beginning in 1639. It starts at the basilica, links 19 chapels and 20 stations on the hills beside the Varduva River, then returns to the church. The stations mainly depict the Passion, the final hours of Jesus’s life leading up to his death on the cross. The founders wanted to recreate Jerusalem, and the town was long nicknamed the New Jerusalem. In early July, the Great Calvary festival lasts up to ten days and attracts tens of thousands of pilgrims: book early.

visits.text: In our view, this is the finest moment of the trip: Zervynos, a village of pine log houses on the banks of the Ūla. Mentioned as early as 1742, it has retained its 18th-century layout. Its sandy soil was poorly suited to growing crops, so the agricultural reforms that reorganized fields and farms elsewhere left it untouched. More than thirty of its buildings are protected. Two old pine trees have cavities carved into them to house bee colonies whose honey was harvested. The village has no stores or restaurants, so bring water and a picnic.

activities.text: Take the trail along the right bank of the Ūla between Zervynos and Mančiagirė. Here, the river flows through an area of inland dunes: sand dunes formed far from the sea, now covered in pines. By cutting into this sand, the Ūla has exposed bare cliffs, the Ūlos skardžiai. In summer, kayakers paddle down the river and through the village. Walk to the cliffs, then return to Zervynos along the same trail.
